The provider labels describe API interfaces, not distinct underlying provider models.\n- The model catalog is a fixed server-side allowlist from the proxy documentation; the documentation does not provide a model-list endpoint.\n- Responses are non-streaming. Streaming is documented by the proxy but is not implemented.\n- Messages are text-only. Attachments, web search, tools, agents, billing, model racing, automatic context compaction, rename/delete, and import/export are not implemented.\n- Context includes completed user/assistant turns plus the current prompt.       "text": "# LiteChat MVP\n\nLiteChat is a private, single-user Django chat application. It provides a browser workspace for text conversations with a small, server-configured set of provider-compatible models. Conversations and messages are stored in SQLite and can be reopened and continued.\n\n## Current Features\n\n- Start a conversation by selecting an enabled provider/model and sending the first prompt.\n- Continue saved conversations using completed messages reconstructed from SQLite as context.\n- Reopen recent conversations from the history list.\n- Select among the documented OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google Gemini proxy interfaces when the corresponding server key is configured.\n- Preserve a submitted prompt when the proxy fails and retry the latest failed response without duplicating that prompt.\n- Receive safe status messages for missing configuration, rate limiting, timeouts, incomplete responses, and proxy failures.\n\n## Important Limitations\n\n- The app has no user accounts or per-user conversation ownership. It must only be exposed behind private access control.\n- The proxy documentation states that all three provider-compatible interfaces currently use DeepSeek Flash. The provider labels describe API interfaces, not distinct underlying provider models.\n- The model catalog is a fixed server-side allowlist from the proxy documentation; the documentation does not provide a model-list endpoint.\n- Responses are non-streaming. Streaming is documented by the proxy but is not implemented.\n- Messages are text-only. Attachments, web search, tools, agents, billing, model racing, automatic context compaction, rename/delete, and import/export are not implemented.\n- Context includes completed user/assistant turns plus the current prompt. Long histories are not automatically truncated or summarized; a proxy/context-size rejection must be handled by starting a shorter conversation.\n- The current requested CodeRange port is `5001`, but another application occupies it. Its LiteChat health/provider endpoints return 404 and LiteChat startup cannot bind; CodeRange routing and static serving are not verified. See the [CodeRange and proxy footgun](footguns/coderange-and-proxy.md).\n\nFor installation and local development, see [Setup](setup.md). For request and persistence boundaries, see [Architecture](architecture.md).",

    "preview": "# CodeRange and Proxy Footguns\n\n## LiteChat Cannot Bind Port 5001 Yet\n\nThe current requested LiteChat port is `5001`, but `127.0.0.1:5001` is occupied by a different application. A startup attempt for LiteChat fails with “That port is already in use”; the listener returns HTTP 404 for LiteChat's `/healthz/` and `/api/providers/` endpoints. TCP reachability therefore does not mean LiteChat is serving there.\n\nEarlier, port `5002` was selected to preserve the incumbent service, and a local Django smoke test there passed. The latest request changes the target back to `5001`; the existing process was not stopped or replaced. Its owner must authorize freeing/reconfiguring `5001`, or the platform must provide a different process/route allocation. No external CodeRange route mapping is available in this workspace. Local Django test-client or loopback success does not verify CodeRange routing.\n\n## Server-Side Proxy Keys\n\nThe proxy docs name `BUILD_OPENAI_KEY`, `BUILD_ANTHROPIC_KEY`, and `BUILD_GOOGLE_KEY`. The app checks the relevant variable and sends it only from Django to the fixed proxy host. `.env.example` values are placeholders, not working keys. All three variables were present in the current execution environment, and live OpenAI-, Anthropic-, and Google-compatible proxy requests each returned HTTP 200 with a complete parsed response. This does not independently verify injection into a separately managed CodeRange worker. Verify worker configuration without printing or sharing values.\n\nNever paste actual key values into Git-tracked files, issue descriptions, logs, frontend configuration, or browser storage. Configure them with the platform's secret/environment mechanism. The app does not load `.env` automatically.\n\n## Provider Labels Are Proxy Interfaces\n\nThe public proxy docs state that the OpenAI-, Anthropic-, and Gemini-compatible interfaces all use DeepSeek Flash and do not reproduce the named providers' model behavior. The UI discloses this. Do not describe the choices as distinct upstream OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google models.\n\nNo model-list endpoint is documented. Deleting a conversation through the ORM cascades to its messages; no delete UI/API is currently exposed.\n29: \n30: New conversations are created lazily on the first prompt. The app stores that prompt and creates a pending assistant message before calling the proxy. On success, the assistant message becomes completed. On proxy failure, the prompt is retained and the assistant message is marked failed. A retry targets the latest failed assistant message and reuses its preceding user prompt.\n31: \n32: Context construction includes only completed user/assistant pairs plus the current user prompt. Failed and incomplete turns are excluded. No model discovery endpoint was found in the proxy docs; the initial model choices are a static allowlist. It makes no automatic retry after an upstream failure. ## Assistant

The root cause is confirmed: Django renders `/static/chat/...` as root-absolute URLs, and the JavaScript API root is also `/api`; both escape the `/proxy/5001/` mount. I’ll keep Django’s upstream `STATIC_URL=/static/` and staticfiles configuration intact, but add a relative document base and make asset/API/home URLs resolve beneath the mounted app path. I’ll add a regression test for the rendered relative asset URLs.

## Assistant

The first configuration test exposed an important Django detail: `staticfiles_storage` normalizes relative `STATIC_URL`, and using `FORCE_SCRIPT_NAME` would make Django’s development static handler expect the proxy prefix on the upstream path. CodeRange strips that prefix before forwarding. I’m keeping the upstream static route at `/static/` and generating browser-relative asset paths under `<base href="./">`; API URLs will resolve from that same base. This matches the proxy’s path-stripping behavior.

      "text": "# CodeRange and Proxy Footguns\n\n## Distinguish Local Port 5001 From CodeRange Reachability\n\nThe prior port-5001 service was stopped only after explicit user authorization. LiteChat now binds `0.0.0.0:5001`, mounted at `/proxy/5001/`. Keep browser asset and API URLs below this prefix: the page uses `<base href=\"./\">`, relative CSS/JavaScript URLs, and an API root derived from `document.baseURI`. Django keeps `STATIC_URL = \"/static/\"` for upstream requests after CodeRange strips `/proxy/5001`.\n\nThe injected `VSCODE_PROXY_URI` pattern `/proxy/{{port}}/` gives the browser URL `https://<workspace-host>.coderange.net/proxy/5001/`. The user reports the page loads. Local checks confirm the rendered CSS/JavaScript URLs stay below the prefix, and both files serve successfully after simulating CodeRange's prefix stripping. Direct external requests from this execution environment return transport errors, so confirm in the browser that CSS, JavaScript, and API requests succeed after a hard refresh. Private-access policy and SQLite persistence across restarts also remain unverified.\n\n## Server-Side Proxy Keys\n\nThe proxy docs name `BUILD_OPENAI_KEY`, `BUILD_ANTHROPIC_KEY`, and `BUILD_GOOGLE_KEY`. The app checks the relevant variable and sends it only from Django to the fixed proxy host. `.env.example` values are placeholders, not working keys. All three variables were present in the current execution environment, and live OpenAI-, Anthropic-, and Google-compatible proxy requests each returned HTTP 200 with a complete parsed response. This does not independently verify injection into a separately managed CodeRange worker. Verify worker configuration without printing or sharing values.\n\nNever paste actual key values into Git-tracked files, issue descriptions, logs, frontend configuration, or browser storage. Configure them with the platform's secret/environment mechanism. The app does not load `.env` automatically.\n\n## Provider Labels Are Proxy Interfaces\n\nThe public proxy docs state that the OpenAI-, Anthropic-, and Gemini-compatible interfaces all use DeepSeek Flash and do not reproduce the named providers' model behavior. The UI discloses this. Do not describe the choices as distinct upstream OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google models.\n\nNo model-list endpoint is documented. Only the three exact model IDs listed in the proxy docs are currently allowlisted. Do not add model names by guessing.\n\n## Private Single-User Deployment\n\nThe application has no built-in authentication or per-user conversation isolation. The user selected private single-user use. Keep the CodeRange route private; do not expose it on a public/shared host without adding authentication and ownership checks.\n\n## Django Deployment Settings\n\n`DJANGO_DEBUG` defaults to false, and production mode refuses to start without `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY`. Configure `DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS` and `DJANGO_CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` for the actual CodeRange hostname. Forwarded HTTPS headers, secure cookies, static serving, and persistent SQLite storage must be matched to the platform's real setup rather than guessed. A local `runserver` check alone does not validate these settings.\n\n## Non-Streaming and Context Limits\n\nThe proxy documents streaming variants, but the MVP intentionally uses whole-response requests. It has no cancellation support. Long histories are sent in full; automatic truncation or summarization is not implemented. If the proxy rejects an oversized context, shorten the conversation rather than silently dropping turns.",

## User

study adding user accounts, profile pages, per-user chat ownership, and billing accounts to the existing LiteChat project.

The current chat functionality is working well and should be preserved.

Use the existing project and the screenshots/reference behavior as product guidance.

Study the feasibility and recommended design for these new features:

1. User accounts
- signup / create account
- login
- logout
- authenticated sessions
- protect the chat workspace from unauthenticated users

2. Per-user chat ownership
- each Conversation belongs to one user
- each user only sees their own chat history
- users cannot open or continue another user's conversation by changing IDs or URLs
- preserve the current working chat/provider/proxy functionality

3. Profile page
The profile should support or display:
- display name
- username
- user ID
- member since date

4. Billing account
Add a billing account page similar to the LiteChat reference.

For the MVP, study a simple internal billing model with:
- one personal billing account per user
- active/inactive status
- available credit balance
- display of billing account name
- no real payment gateway yet
- no credit-card processing
- no automatic purchases unless explicitly added later

Study an appropriate Django model for this, such as a BillingAccount related one-to-one with the user.

5. Navigation/UI
Study how the current LiteChat sidebar could include:
- Chat
- My Profile
- Billing Account
- Logout

Keep the existing chat UI and functionality intact.

6. Existing data migration
The current database may contain conversations created before user accounts existed.

Study safe options for assigning or handling those existing conversations.

Do not silently choose a destructive migration strategy.

7. Security
Study:
- Django authentication
- password hashing
- session authentication
- login protection
- cross-user conversation isolation
- IDOR protection
- CSRF
- profile ownership
- billing data ownership

8. Testing
Include recommended tests for:
- signup
- login
- logout
- protected pages
- profile access
- profile updates
- global system prompt persistence
- billing account creation/display
- conversation ownership
- cross-user access rejection
- preserving existing chat functionality

- write the study to `doc/study/{unix_timestamp}_accounts-profile-billing.md`
- only modify the study document unless the directory must be created

- stop after completing the study

Model output is inserted as text, not HTML.\n29: \n30: ## Persistence and Context\n31: \n32: `Conversation` stores title, current provider/model selection, and timestamps. `Message` stores role, text content, status, provider/model attribution for assistant turns, and a safe failure category. Deleting a conversation through the ORM cascades to its messages; no delete UI/API is currently exposed.\n33: \n34: New conversations are created lazily on the first prompt. On proxy failure, the prompt is retained and the assistant message is marked failed. A retry targets the latest failed assistant message and reuses its preceding user prompt.\n35: \n36: Context construction includes only completed user/assistant pairs plus the current user prompt. It makes no automatic retry after an upstream failure. Proxy statuses are mapped to safe app errors; raw upstream bodies, headers, and keys are not returned to the browser.\n51: \n52: Source: <https://proxy.litechat.ai/docs>, <https://proxy.litechat.ai/docs/openai/chat-completions>, <https://proxy.litechat.ai/docs/anthropic/messages>, <https://proxy.litechat.ai/docs/google/gemini>.\n53: \n54: ## Privacy Boundary\n55: \n56: This is a private single-user app with no built-in authentication or user ownership fields. The CodeRange proxy must remove `/proxy/5001` before forwarding requests so Django receives `/static/...` and `/api/...`; local checks simulated this mapping, but post-fix browser delivery was not independently verified in this session.\n\n## Django Areas\n\n- `config/settings.py`: Django, SQLite, environment settings, templates, and static files.\n- `config/urls.py`: chat page, health endpoint, and API routes.\n- `chat/models.py`: `Conversation` and `Message` persistence.\n- `chat/providers.py`: fixed, documented provider/model allowlist and server-side key-presence status.\n- `chat/services/conversations.py`: input validation, lazy conversation creation, ordered context reconstruction, pending/failed turn state, completion persistence, and explicit retry.\n- `chat/services/proxy_client.py`: verified provider-specific URL, header, request-body, response-body, and failure mapping.\n- `chat/views.py` and `chat/urls.py`: same-origin JSON endpoints with Django CSRF middleware.\n- `templates/chat/index.html` and `static/chat/`: responsive workspace and DOM updates. Model output is inserted as text, not HTML.\n\n## Persistence and Context\n\n`Conversation` stores title, current provider/model selection, and timestamps. `Message` stores role, text content, status, provider/model attribution for assistant turns, and a safe failure category. Deleting a conversation through the ORM cascades to its messages; no delete UI/API is currently exposed.\n\nNew conversations are created lazily on the first prompt. The app stores that prompt and creates a pending assistant message before calling the proxy. On success, the assistant message becomes completed. On proxy failure, the prompt is retained and the assistant message is marked failed. A retry targets the latest failed assistant message and reuses its preceding user prompt.\n\nContext construction includes only completed user/assistant pairs plus the current user prompt. Failed and incomplete turns are excluded. The entire eligible history is sent each time; token-window compaction is not implemented.\n\n## Proxy Contract\n\nThe proxy's public docs (revision 2026-09-19) document separate formats rather than one normalized endpoint:\n\n| Interface | Endpoint | Authentication | Allowlisted model |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| OpenAI Chat Completions | `POST /openai/v1/chat/completions` | `Authorization: Bearer` using `BUILD_OPENAI_KEY` | `gpt-5.6-luna` |\n| Anthropic Messages | `POST /anthropic/v1/messages` | `x-api-key` using `BUILD_ANTHROPIC_KEY`, plus `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01` | `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` |\n| Google Gemini Generate Content | `POST /google/v1beta/models/gemini-3.8-flash:generateContent` | `x-goog-api-key` using `BUILD_GOOGLE_KEY` | `gemini-3.8-flash` |\n\nThe app maps the same internal ordered text turns to each documented request shape and parses each response separately. No model discovery endpoint was found in the proxy docs; the initial model choices are a static allowlist. The proxy says all three interfaces currently use DeepSeek Flash, so these names are interface/model identifiers and do not indicate three distinct upstream model implementations.\n\nThe app uses non-streaming requests with a 90-second timeout and a 2,000,000-byte response limit. It makes no automatic retry after an upstream failure. Proxy statuses are mapped to safe app errors; raw upstream bodies, headers, and keys are not returned to the browser.\n\nSource: <https://proxy.litechat.ai/docs>, <https://proxy.litechat.ai/docs/openai/chat-completions>, <https://proxy.litechat.ai/docs/anthropic/messages>, <https://proxy.litechat.ai/docs/google/gemini>.\n\n## Privacy Boundary\n\nThis is a private single-user app with no built-in authentication or user ownership fields. Every conversation in the SQLite database is visible to anyone who can reach this app. It must be deployed behind private access control. CodeRange's actual access-control and TLS/reverse-proxy behavior has not yet been verified.",

      "text": "from django.db import IntegrityError, transaction\nfrom django.test import TestCase\n\nfrom chat.models import Conversation, Message\n\n\nclass WorkspaceFoundationTests(TestCase):\n    def test_home_page_renders_workspace(self):\n        response = self.client.get(\"/\")\n\n        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)\n        self.assertContains(response, \"LiteChat\")\n        self.assertContains(response, \"New conversation\")\n\n    def test_health_check_returns_ok(self):\n        response = self.client.get(\"/healthz/\")\n\n        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)\n        self.assertEqual(response.json(), {\"status\": \"ok\"})\n\n    def test_conversation_delete_cascades_to_messages(self):\n        conversation = Conversation.objects.create(\n            title=\"A thread\",\n            provider=\"openai\",\n            model_id=\"gpt-5.6-luna\",\n        )\n        first = Message.objects.create(\n            conversation=conversation,\n            role=Message.Role.USER,\n            content=\"Prompt\",\n        )\n        second = Message.objects.create(\n            conversation=conversation,\n            role=Message.Role.ASSISTANT,\n            content=\"Reply\",\n            provider=\"openai\",\n            model_id=\"gpt-5.6-luna\",\n        )\n\n        self.assertEqual(list(conversation.messages.all()), [first, second])\n        conversation.delete()\n        self.assertEqual(Message.objects.count(), 0)\n\n    def test_message_role_is_constrained_in_database(self):\n        conversation = Conversation.objects.create(\n            title=\"A thread\",\n            provider=\"openai\",\n            model_id=\"gpt-5.6-luna\",\n        )\n\n        with self.assertRaises(IntegrityError), transaction.atomic():\n            Message.objects.create(\n                conversation=conversation,\n                role=\"system\",\n                content=\"Not an allowed role\",\n            )",

[1.8](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/1.8/topics/auth/default/)\n\n-   [](#top)\n\n# Using the Django authentication system[¶](#using-the-django-authentication-system \"Link to this heading\")\n\nThis document explains the usage of Django’s authentication system in its default configuration. This configuration has evolved to serve the most common project needs, handling a reasonably wide range of tasks, and has a careful implementation of passwords and permissions. For projects where authentication needs differ from the default, Django supports extensive [extension and customization](../customizing/) of authentication.\n\nDjango authentication provides both authentication and authorization together and is generally referred to as the authentication system, as these features are somewhat coupled.\n\n## `User` objects[¶](#user-objects \"Link to this heading\")\n\n[`User`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User \"django.contrib.auth.models.User\") objects are the core of the authentication system. They typically represent the people interacting with your site and are used to enable things like restricting access, registering user profiles, associating content with creators etc. Only one class of user exists in Django’s authentication framework, i.e., [`'superusers'`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User.is_superuser \"django.contrib.auth.models.User.is_superuser\") or admin [`'staff'`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User.is_staff \"django.contrib.auth.models.User.is_staff\") users are just user objects with special attributes set, not different classes of user objects.\n\nThe primary attributes of the default user are:\n\n-   [`username`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User.username \"django.contrib.auth.models.User.username\")\n    \n-   [`password`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User.password \"django.contrib.auth.models.User.password\")\n    \n-   [`email`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User.email \"django.contrib.auth.models.User.email\")\n    \n-   [`first_name`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User.first_name \"django.contrib.auth.models.User.first_name\")\n    \n-   [`last_name`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User.last_name \"django.contrib.auth.models.User.last_name\")\n    \n\nSee the [`full API documentation`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User \"django.contrib.auth.models.User\") for full reference, the documentation that follows is more task oriented.\n\n### Creating users[¶](#creating-users \"Link to this heading\")\n\nThe most direct way to create users is to use the included [`create_user()`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.UserManager.create_user \"django.contrib.auth.models.UserManager.create_user\") helper function:\n\n\\>>> from django.contrib.auth.models import User\n\\>>> user \\= User.objects.create\\_user(\"john\", \"lennon@thebeatles.com\", \"johnpassword\")\n\n\\# At this point, user is a User object that has already been saved\n\\# to the database. You can continue to change its attributes\n\\# if you want to change other fields.\n\\>>> user.last\\_name \\= \"Lennon\"\n\\>>> user.save()\n\nIf you have the Django admin installed, you can also [create users interactively](#auth-admin).\n\n### Creating superusers[¶](#creating-superusers \"Link to this heading\")\n\nCreate superusers using the [`createsuperuser`](../../../ref/django-admin/#django-admin-createsuperuser) command:\n\n /  \n\n$ python manage.py createsuperuser \\--username\\=joe \\--email\\=joe@example.com\n\n...\\\\> py manage.py createsuperuser --username=joe --email=joe@example.com\n\nYou will be prompted for a password. After you enter one, the user will be created immediately. If you leave off the [`--username`](../../../ref/django-admin/#cmdoption-createsuperuser-username) or [`--email`](../../../ref/django-admin/#cmdoption-createsuperuser-email) options, it will prompt you for those values.\n\n### Changing passwords[¶](#changing-passwords \"Link to this heading\")\n\nDjango does not store raw (clear text) passwords on the user model, but only a hash (see [documentation of how passwords are managed](../passwords/) for full details). Because of this, do not attempt to manipulate the password attribute of the user directly. This is why a helper function is used when creating a user.\n\nTo change a user’s password, you have several options:\n\n[`manage.py changepassword *username*`](../../../ref/django-admin/#django-admin-changepassword) offers a method of changing a user’s password from the command line. It prompts you to change the password of a given user which you must enter twice. If they both match, the new password will be changed immediately. If you do not supply a user, the command will attempt to change the password whose username matches the current system user.\n\nYou can also change a password programmatically, using [`set_password()`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User.set_password \"django.contrib.auth.models.User.set_password\"):\n\n\\>>> from django.contrib.auth.models import User\n\\>>> u \\= User.objects.get(username\\=\"john\")\n\\>>> u.set\\_password(\"new password\")\n\\>>> u.save()\n\nIf you have the Django admin installed, you can also change user’s passwords on the [authentication system’s admin pages](#auth-admin).\n\nDjango also provides [views](#built-in-auth-views) and [forms](#built-in-auth-forms) that may be used to allow users to change their own passwords.\n\nChanging a user’s password will log out all their sessions. See [Session invalidation on password change](#session-invalidation-on-password-change) for details.\n\n### Authenticating users[¶](#authenticating-users \"Link to this heading\")\n\nauthenticate(*request\\=None*, *\\*\\*credentials*)[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/__init__.py#L108)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.authenticate \"Link to this definition\")\n\naauthenticate(*request\\=None*, *\\*\\*credentials*)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.aauthenticate \"Link to this definition\")\n\n*Asynchronous version*: `aauthenticate()`\n\nUse [`authenticate()`](#django.contrib.auth.authenticate \"django.contrib.auth.authenticate\") to verify a set of credentials. It takes credentials as keyword arguments, `username` and `password` for the default case, checks them against each [authentication backend](../customizing/#authentication-backends), and returns a [`User`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User \"django.contrib.auth.models.User\") object if the credentials are valid for a backend. If the credentials aren’t valid for any backend or if a backend raises [`PermissionDenied`](../../../ref/exceptions/#django.core.exceptions.PermissionDenied \"django.core.exceptions.PermissionDenied\"), it returns `None`. For example:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth import authenticate\n\nuser \\= authenticate(username\\=\"john\", password\\=\"secret\")\nif user is not None:\n    \\# A backend authenticated the credentials\n    ...\nelse:\n    \\# No backend authenticated the credentials\n    ...\n\n`request` is an optional [`HttpRequest`](../../../ref/request-response/#django.http.HttpRequest \"django.http.HttpRequest\") which is passed on the `authenticate()` method of the authentication backends.\n\nNote\n\nThis is a low level way to authenticate a set of credentials; for example, it’s used by the [`RemoteUserMiddleware`](../../../ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.RemoteUserMiddleware \"django.contrib.auth.middleware.RemoteUserMiddleware\"). Unless you are writing your own authentication system, you probably won’t use this. Rather if you’re looking for a way to login a user, use the [`LoginView`](#django.contrib.auth.views.LoginView \"django.contrib.auth.views.LoginView\").\n\n## Permissions and Authorization[¶](#permissions-and-authorization \"Link to this heading\")\n\nDjango comes with a built-in permissions system. It provides a way to assign permissions to specific users and groups of users.\n\nIt’s used by the Django admin site, but you’re welcome to use it in your own code.\n\nThe Django admin site uses permissions as follows:\n\n-   Access to view objects is limited to users with the “view” or “change” permission for that type of object.\n    \n-   Access to view the “add” form and add an object is limited to users with the “add” permission for that type of object.\n    \n-   Access to view the change list, view the “change” form and change an object is limited to users with the “change” permission for that type of object.\n    \n-   Access to delete an object is limited to users with the “delete” permission for that type of object.\n    \n\nPermissions can be set not only per type of object, but also per specific object instance. By using the [`has_view_permission()`](../../../ref/contrib/admin/#django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin.has_view_permission \"django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin.has_view_permission\"), [`has_add_permission()`](../../../ref/contrib/admin/#django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin.has_add_permission \"django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin.has_add_permission\"), [`has_change_permission()`](../../../ref/contrib/admin/#django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin.has_change_permission \"django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin.has_change_permission\") and [`has_delete_permission()`](../../../ref/contrib/admin/#django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin.has_delete_permission \"django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin.has_delete_permission\") methods provided by the [`ModelAdmin`](../../../ref/contrib/admin/#django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin \"django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin\") class, it is possible to customize permissions for different object instances of the same type.\n\n[`User`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User \"django.contrib.auth.models.User\") objects have two many-to-many fields: `groups` and `user_permissions`. [`User`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User \"django.contrib.auth.models.User\") objects can access their related objects in the same way as any other [Django model](../../db/models/):\n\nmyuser.groups.set(\\[group\\_list\\])\nmyuser.groups.add(group, group, ...)\nmyuser.groups.remove(group, group, ...)\nmyuser.groups.clear()\nmyuser.user\\_permissions.set(\\[permission\\_list\\])\nmyuser.user\\_permissions.add(permission, permission, ...)\nmyuser.user\\_permissions.remove(permission, permission, ...)\nmyuser.user\\_permissions.clear()\n\n### Default permissions[¶](#default-permissions \"Link to this heading\")\n\nWhen `django.contrib.auth` is listed in your [`INSTALLED_APPS`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-INSTALLED_APPS) setting, it will ensure that four default permissions – add, change, delete, and view – are created for each Django model defined in one of your installed applications.\n\nThese permissions will be created when you run [`manage.py migrate`](../../../ref/django-admin/#django-admin-migrate); the first time you run `migrate` after adding `django.contrib.auth` to [`INSTALLED_APPS`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-INSTALLED_APPS), the default permissions will be created for all previously-installed models, as well as for any new models being installed at that time. Afterward, it will create default permissions for new models each time you run [`manage.py migrate`](../../../ref/django-admin/#django-admin-migrate) (the function that creates permissions is connected to the [`post_migrate`](../../../ref/signals/#django.db.models.signals.post_migrate \"django.db.models.signals.post_migrate\") signal).\n\nAssuming you have an application with an [`app_label`](../../../ref/models/options/#django.db.models.Options.app_label \"django.db.models.Options.app_label\") `foo` and a model named `Bar`, to test for basic permissions you should use:\n\n-   add: `user.has_perm('foo.add_bar')`\n    \n-   change: `user.has_perm('foo.change_bar')`\n    \n-   delete: `user.has_perm('foo.delete_bar')`\n    \n-   view: `user.has_perm('foo.view_bar')`\n    \n\nThe [`Permission`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.Permission \"django.contrib.auth.models.Permission\") model is rarely accessed directly.\n\n### Groups[¶](#groups \"Link to this heading\")\n\n[`django.contrib.auth.models.Group`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.Group \"django.contrib.auth.models.Group\") models are a generic way of categorizing users so you can apply permissions, or some other label, to those users. A user can belong to any number of groups.\n\nA user in a group automatically has the permissions granted to that group. For example, if the group `Site editors` has the permission `can_edit_home_page`, any user in that group will have that permission.\n\nBeyond permissions, groups are a convenient way to categorize users to give them some label, or extended functionality. For example, you could create a group `'Special users'`, and you could write code that could, say, give them access to a members-only portion of your site, or send them members-only email messages.\n\n### Programmatically creating permissions[¶](#programmatically-creating-permissions \"Link to this heading\")\n\nWhile [custom permissions](../customizing/#custom-permissions) can be defined within a model’s `Meta` class, you can also create permissions directly. For example, you can create the `can_publish` permission for a `BlogPost` model in `myapp`:\n\nfrom myapp.models import BlogPost\nfrom django.contrib.auth.models import Permission\nfrom django.contrib.contenttypes.models import ContentType\n\ncontent\\_type \\= ContentType.objects.get\\_for\\_model(BlogPost)\npermission \\= Permission.objects.create(\n    codename\\=\"can\\_publish\",\n    name\\=\"Can Publish Posts\",\n    content\\_type\\=content\\_type,\n)\n\nThe permission can then be assigned to a [`User`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User \"django.contrib.auth.models.User\") via its `user_permissions` attribute or to a [`Group`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.Group \"django.contrib.auth.models.Group\") via its `permissions` attribute.\n\nProxy models need their own content type\n\nIf you want to create [permissions for a proxy model](#proxy-models-permissions-topic), pass `for_concrete_model=False` to [`ContentTypeManager.get_for_model()`](../../../ref/contrib/contenttypes/#django.contrib.contenttypes.models.ContentTypeManager.get_for_model \"django.contrib.contenttypes.models.ContentTypeManager.get_for_model\") to get the appropriate `ContentType`:\n\ncontent\\_type \\= ContentType.objects.get\\_for\\_model(\n    BlogPostProxy, for\\_concrete\\_model\\=False\n)\n\n### Permission caching[¶](#permission-caching \"Link to this heading\")\n\nThe [`ModelBackend`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.backends.ModelBackend \"django.contrib.auth.backends.ModelBackend\") caches permissions on the user object after the first time they need to be fetched for a permissions check. This is typically fine for the request-response cycle since permissions aren’t typically checked immediately after they are added (in the admin, for example). If you are adding permissions and checking them immediately afterward, in a test or view for example, the easiest solution is to re-fetch the user from the database. For example:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth.models import Permission, User\nfrom django.contrib.contenttypes.models import ContentType\nfrom django.shortcuts import get\\_object\\_or\\_404\n\nfrom myapp.models import BlogPost\n\ndef user\\_gains\\_perms(request, user\\_id):\n    user \\= get\\_object\\_or\\_404(User, pk\\=user\\_id)\n    \\# any permission check will cache the current set of permissions\n    user.has\\_perm(\"myapp.change\\_blogpost\")\n\n    content\\_type \\= ContentType.objects.get\\_for\\_model(BlogPost)\n    permission \\= Permission.objects.get(\n        codename\\=\"change\\_blogpost\",\n        content\\_type\\=content\\_type,\n    )\n    user.user\\_permissions.add(permission)\n\n    \\# Checking the cached permission set\n    user.has\\_perm(\"myapp.change\\_blogpost\")  \\# False\n\n    \\# Request new instance of User\n    \\# Be aware that user.refresh\\_from\\_db() won't clear the cache.\n    user \\= get\\_object\\_or\\_404(User, pk\\=user\\_id)\n\n    \\# Permission cache is repopulated from the database\n    user.has\\_perm(\"myapp.change\\_blogpost\")  \\# True\n\n    ...\n\n### Proxy models[¶](#proxy-models \"Link to this heading\")\n\nProxy models work exactly the same way as concrete models. Permissions are created using the own content type of the proxy model. Proxy models don’t inherit the permissions of the concrete model they subclass:\n\nclass Person(models.Model):\n    class Meta:\n        permissions \\= \\[(\"can\\_eat\\_pizzas\", \"Can eat pizzas\")\\]\n\nclass Student(Person):\n    class Meta:\n        proxy \\= True\n        permissions \\= \\[(\"can\\_deliver\\_pizzas\", \"Can deliver pizzas\")\\]\n\n\\>>> \\# Fetch the content type for the proxy model.\n\\>>> content\\_type \\= ContentType.objects.get\\_for\\_model(Student, for\\_concrete\\_model\\=False)\n\\>>> student\\_permissions \\= Permission.objects.filter(content\\_type\\=content\\_type)\n\\>>> \\[p.codename for p in student\\_permissions\\]\n\\['add\\_student', 'change\\_student', 'delete\\_student', 'view\\_student',\n'can\\_deliver\\_pizzas'\\]\n\\>>> for permission in student\\_permissions:\n...     user.user\\_permissions.add(permission)\n...\n\\>>> user.has\\_perm(\"app.add\\_person\")\nFalse\n\\>>> user.has\\_perm(\"app.can\\_eat\\_pizzas\")\nFalse\n\\>>> user.has\\_perms((\"app.add\\_student\", \"app.can\\_deliver\\_pizzas\"))\nTrue\n\n## Authentication in web requests[¶](#authentication-in-web-requests \"Link to this heading\")\n\nDjango uses [sessions](../../http/sessions/) and middleware to hook the authentication system into [`request objects`](../../../ref/request-response/#django.http.HttpRequest \"django.http.HttpRequest\").\n\nThese provide a [`request.user`](../../../ref/request-response/#django.http.HttpRequest.user \"django.http.HttpRequest.user\") attribute and a [`request.auser`](../../../ref/request-response/#django.http.HttpRequest.auser \"django.http.HttpRequest.auser\") async method on every request which represents the current user. If the current user has not logged in, this attribute will be set to an instance of [`AnonymousUser`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.AnonymousUser \"django.contrib.auth.models.AnonymousUser\"), otherwise it will be an instance of [`User`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User \"django.contrib.auth.models.User\").\n\nYou can tell them apart with [`is_authenticated`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User.is_authenticated \"django.contrib.auth.models.User.is_authenticated\"), like so:\n\nif request.user.is\\_authenticated:\n    \\# Do something for authenticated users.\n    ...\nelse:\n    \\# Do something for anonymous users.\n    ...\n\nOr in an asynchronous view:\n\nuser \\= await request.auser()\nif user.is\\_authenticated:\n    \\# Do something for authenticated users.\n    ...\nelse:\n    \\# Do something for anonymous users.\n    ...\n\n### How to log a user in[¶](#how-to-log-a-user-in \"Link to this heading\")\n\nIf you have an authenticated user you want to attach to the current session - this is done with a [`login()`](#django.contrib.auth.login \"django.contrib.auth.login\") function.\n\nlogin(*request*, *user*, *backend\\=None*)[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/__init__.py#L153)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.login \"Link to this definition\")\n\nalogin(*request*, *user*, *backend\\=None*)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.alogin \"Link to this definition\")\n\n*Asynchronous version*: `alogin()`\n\nTo log a user in, from a view, use [`login()`](#django.contrib.auth.login \"django.contrib.auth.login\"). It takes an [`HttpRequest`](../../../ref/request-response/#django.http.HttpRequest \"django.http.HttpRequest\") object and a [`User`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User \"django.contrib.auth.models.User\") object. [`login()`](#django.contrib.auth.login \"django.contrib.auth.login\") saves the user’s ID in the session, using Django’s session framework.\n\nNote that any data set during the anonymous session is retained in the session after a user logs in.\n\nThis example shows how you might use both [`authenticate()`](#django.contrib.auth.authenticate \"django.contrib.auth.authenticate\") and [`login()`](#django.contrib.auth.login \"django.contrib.auth.login\"):\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth import authenticate, login\n\ndef my\\_view(request):\n    username \\= request.POST\\[\"username\"\\]\n    password \\= request.POST\\[\"password\"\\]\n    user \\= authenticate(request, username\\=username, password\\=password)\n    if user is not None:\n        login(request, user)\n        \\# Redirect to a success page.\n        ...\n    else:\n        \\# Return an 'invalid login' error message.\n        ...\n\n#### Selecting the authentication backend[¶](#selecting-the-authentication-backend \"Link to this heading\")\n\nWhen a user logs in, the user’s ID and the backend that was used for authentication are saved in the user’s session. This allows the same [authentication backend](../customizing/#authentication-backends) to fetch the user’s details on a future request. The authentication backend to save in the session is selected as follows:\n\n1.  Use the value of the optional `backend` argument, if provided.\n    \n2.  Use the value of the `user.backend` attribute, if present. This allows pairing [`authenticate()`](#django.contrib.auth.authenticate \"django.contrib.auth.authenticate\") and [`login()`](#django.contrib.auth.login \"django.contrib.auth.login\"): [`authenticate()`](#django.contrib.auth.authenticate \"django.contrib.auth.authenticate\") sets the `user.backend` attribute on the user object it returns.\n    \n3.  Use the `backend` in [`AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS), if there is only one.\n    \n4.  Otherwise, raise an exception.\n    \n\nIn cases 1 and 2, the value of the `backend` argument or the `user.backend` attribute should be a dotted import path string (like that found in [`AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS)), not the actual backend class.\n\n### How to log a user out[¶](#how-to-log-a-user-out \"Link to this heading\")\n\nlogout(*request*)[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/__init__.py#L243)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.logout \"Link to this definition\")\n\nalogout(*request*)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.alogout \"Link to this definition\")\n\n*Asynchronous version*: `alogout()`\n\nTo log out a user who has been logged in via [`django.contrib.auth.login()`](#django.contrib.auth.login \"django.contrib.auth.login\"), use [`django.contrib.auth.logout()`](#django.contrib.auth.logout \"django.contrib.auth.logout\") within your view. It takes an [`HttpRequest`](../../../ref/request-response/#django.http.HttpRequest \"django.http.HttpRequest\") object and has no return value. Example:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth import logout\n\ndef logout\\_view(request):\n    logout(request)\n    \\# Redirect to a success page.\n\nNote that [`logout()`](#django.contrib.auth.logout \"django.contrib.auth.logout\") doesn’t throw any errors if the user wasn’t logged in.\n\nWhen you call [`logout()`](#django.contrib.auth.logout \"django.contrib.auth.logout\"), the session data for the current request is completely cleaned out. All existing data is removed. This is to prevent another person from using the same web browser to log in and have access to the previous user’s session data. If you want to put anything into the session that will be available to the user immediately after logging out, do that *after* calling [`django.contrib.auth.logout()`](#django.contrib.auth.logout \"django.contrib.auth.logout\").\n\n### Limiting access to logged-in users[¶](#limiting-access-to-logged-in-users \"Link to this heading\")\n\n#### The raw way[¶](#the-raw-way \"Link to this heading\")\n\nThe raw way to limit access to pages is to check [`request.user.is_authenticated`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User.is_authenticated \"django.contrib.auth.models.User.is_authenticated\") and either redirect to a login page:\n\nfrom django.conf import settings\nfrom django.shortcuts import redirect\n\ndef my\\_view(request):\n    if not request.user.is\\_authenticated:\n        return redirect(f\"{settings.LOGIN\\_URL}?next={request.path}\")\n    \\# ...\n\n…or display an error message:\n\nfrom django.shortcuts import render\n\ndef my\\_view(request):\n    if not request.user.is\\_authenticated:\n        return render(request, \"myapp/login\\_error.html\")\n    \\# ...\n\n#### The `login_required` decorator[¶](#the-login-required-decorator \"Link to this heading\")\n\nlogin\\_required(*redirect\\_field\\_name\\='next'*, *login\\_url\\=None*)[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/decorators.py#L71)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required \"Link to this definition\")\n\nAs a shortcut, you can use the convenient [`login_required()`](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required \"django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required\") decorator:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth.decorators import login\\_required\n\n@login\\_required\ndef my\\_view(request): ...\n\n[`login_required()`](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required \"django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required\") does the following:\n\n-   If the user isn’t logged in, redirect to [`settings.LOGIN_URL`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-LOGIN_URL), passing the current absolute path in the query string. Example: `/accounts/login/?next=/polls/3/`.\n    \n-   If the user is logged in, execute the view normally. The view code is free to assume the user is logged in.\n    \n\nBy default, the path that the user should be redirected to upon successful authentication is stored in a query string parameter called `\"next\"`. If you would prefer to use a different name for this parameter, [`login_required()`](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required \"django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required\") takes an optional `redirect_field_name` parameter:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth.decorators import login\\_required\n\n@login\\_required(redirect\\_field\\_name\\=\"my\\_redirect\\_field\")\ndef my\\_view(request): ...\n\nNote that if you provide a value to `redirect_field_name`, you will most likely need to customize your login template as well, since the template context variable which stores the redirect path will use the value of `redirect_field_name` as its key rather than `\"next\"` (the default).\n\n[`login_required()`](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required \"django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required\") also takes an optional `login_url` parameter. Example:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth.decorators import login\\_required\n\n@login\\_required(login\\_url\\=\"/accounts/login/\")\ndef my\\_view(request): ...\n\nNote that if you don’t specify the `login_url` parameter, you’ll need to ensure that the [`settings.LOGIN_URL`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-LOGIN_URL) and your login view are properly associated. For example, using the defaults, add the following lines to your URLconf:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth import views as auth\\_views\n\npath(\"accounts/login/\", auth\\_views.LoginView.as\\_view()),\n\nThe [`settings.LOGIN_URL`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-LOGIN_URL) also accepts view function names and [named URL patterns](../../http/urls/#naming-url-patterns). This allows you to freely remap your login view within your URLconf without having to update the setting.\n\nNote\n\nThe `login_required` decorator does NOT check the `is_active` flag on a user, but the default [`AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS) reject inactive users.\n\nSee also\n\nIf you are writing custom views for Django’s admin (or need the same authorization check that the built-in views use), you may find the [`django.contrib.admin.views.decorators.staff_member_required()`](../../../ref/contrib/admin/#django.contrib.admin.views.decorators.staff_member_required \"django.contrib.admin.views.decorators.staff_member_required\") decorator a useful alternative to `login_required()`.\n\nChanged in Django 5.1:\n\nSupport for wrapping asynchronous view functions was added.\n\n#### The `LoginRequiredMixin` mixin[¶](#the-loginrequiredmixin-mixin \"Link to this heading\")\n\nWhen using [class-based views](../../class-based-views/), you can achieve the same behavior as with `login_required` by using the `LoginRequiredMixin`. This mixin should be at the leftmost position in the inheritance list.\n\n*class* LoginRequiredMixin[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/mixins.py#L67)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.LoginRequiredMixin \"Link to this definition\")\n\nIf a view is using this mixin, all requests by non-authenticated users will be redirected to the login page or shown an HTTP 403 Forbidden error, depending on the [`raise_exception`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.raise_exception \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.raise_exception\") parameter.\n\nYou can set any of the parameters of [`AccessMixin`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin\") to customize the handling of unauthorized users:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth.mixins import LoginRequiredMixin\n\nclass MyView(LoginRequiredMixin, View):\n    login\\_url \\= \"/login/\"\n    redirect\\_field\\_name \\= \"redirect\\_to\"\n\nNote\n\nJust as the `login_required` decorator, this mixin does NOT check the `is_active` flag on a user, but the default [`AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS) reject inactive users.\n\n#### The `login_not_required` decorator[¶](#the-login-not-required-decorator \"Link to this heading\")\n\nNew in Django 5.1.\n\nWhen [`LoginRequiredMiddleware`](../../../ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware \"django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware\") is installed, all views require authentication by default. Some views, such as the login view, may need to disable this behavior.\n\nlogin\\_not\\_required()[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/decorators.py#L88)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_not_required \"Link to this definition\")\n\nAllows unauthenticated requests to this view when [`LoginRequiredMiddleware`](../../../ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware \"django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware\") is installed.\n\n#### Limiting access to logged-in users that pass a test[¶](#limiting-access-to-logged-in-users-that-pass-a-test \"Link to this heading\")\n\nTo limit access based on certain permissions or some other test, you’d do essentially the same thing as described in the previous section.\n\nYou can run your test on [`request.user`](../../../ref/request-response/#django.http.HttpRequest.user \"django.http.HttpRequest.user\") in the view directly. For example, this view checks to make sure the user has an email in the desired domain and if not, redirects to the login page:\n\nfrom django.shortcuts import redirect\n\ndef my\\_view(request):\n    if not request.user.email.endswith(\"@example.com\"):\n        return redirect(\"/login/?next=%s\" % request.path)\n    \\# ...\n\nuser\\_passes\\_test(*test\\_func*, *login\\_url\\=None*, *redirect\\_field\\_name\\='next'*)[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/decorators.py#L12)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.user_passes_test \"Link to this definition\")\n\nAs a shortcut, you can use the convenient `user_passes_test` decorator which performs a redirect when the callable returns `False`:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth.decorators import user\\_passes\\_test\n\ndef email\\_check(user):\n    return user.email.endswith(\"@example.com\")\n\n@user\\_passes\\_test(email\\_check)\ndef my\\_view(request): ...\n\n[`user_passes_test()`](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.user_passes_test \"django.contrib.auth.decorators.user_passes_test\") takes a required argument: a callable that takes a [`User`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User \"django.contrib.auth.models.User\") object and returns `True` if the user is allowed to view the page. Note that [`user_passes_test()`](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.user_passes_test \"django.contrib.auth.decorators.user_passes_test\") does not automatically check that the [`User`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User \"django.contrib.auth.models.User\") is not anonymous.\n\n[`user_passes_test()`](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.user_passes_test \"django.contrib.auth.decorators.user_passes_test\") takes two optional arguments:\n\n`login_url`\n\nLets you specify the URL that users who don’t pass the test will be redirected to. It may be a login page and defaults to [`settings.LOGIN_URL`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-LOGIN_URL) if you don’t specify one.\n\n`redirect_field_name`\n\nSame as for [`login_required()`](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required \"django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required\"). Setting it to `None` removes it from the URL, which you may want to do if you are redirecting users that don’t pass the test to a non-login page where there’s no “next page”.\n\nFor example:\n\n@user\\_passes\\_test(email\\_check, login\\_url\\=\"/login/\")\ndef my\\_view(request): ...\n\nChanged in Django 5.1:\n\nSupport for wrapping asynchronous view functions and using asynchronous test callables was added.\n\n*class* UserPassesTestMixin[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/mixins.py#L112)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.UserPassesTestMixin \"Link to this definition\")\n\nWhen using [class-based views](../../class-based-views/), you can use the `UserPassesTestMixin` to do this.\n\ntest\\_func()[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/mixins.py#L118)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.UserPassesTestMixin.test_func \"Link to this definition\")\n\nYou have to override the `test_func()` method of the class to provide the test that is performed. Furthermore, you can set any of the parameters of [`AccessMixin`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin\") to customize the handling of unauthorized users:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth.mixins import UserPassesTestMixin\n\nclass MyView(UserPassesTestMixin, View):\n    def test\\_func(self):\n        return self.request.user.email.endswith(\"@example.com\")\n\nget\\_test\\_func()[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/mixins.py#L125)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.UserPassesTestMixin.get_test_func \"Link to this definition\")\n\nYou can also override the `get_test_func()` method to have the mixin use a differently named function for its checks (instead of [`test_func()`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.UserPassesTestMixin.test_func \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.UserPassesTestMixin.test_func\")).\n\nStacking `UserPassesTestMixin`\n\nDue to the way `UserPassesTestMixin` is implemented, you cannot stack them in your inheritance list. The following does NOT work:\n\nclass TestMixin1(UserPassesTestMixin):\n    def test\\_func(self):\n        return self.request.user.email.endswith(\"@example.com\")\n\nclass TestMixin2(UserPassesTestMixin):\n    def test\\_func(self):\n        return self.request.user.username.startswith(\"django\")\n\nclass MyView(TestMixin1, TestMixin2, View): ...\n\nIf `TestMixin1` would call `super()` and take that result into account, `TestMixin1` wouldn’t work standalone anymore.\n\n#### The `permission_required` decorator[¶](#the-permission-required-decorator \"Link to this heading\")\n\npermission\\_required(*perm*, *login\\_url\\=None*, *raise\\_exception\\=False*)[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/decorators.py#L96)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.permission_required \"Link to this definition\")\n\nIt’s a relatively common task to check whether a user has a particular permission. For that reason, Django provides a shortcut for that case: the [`permission_required()`](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.permission_required \"django.contrib.auth.decorators.permission_required\") decorator:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth.decorators import permission\\_required\n\n@permission\\_required(\"polls.add\\_choice\")\ndef my\\_view(request): ...\n\nJust like the [`has_perm()`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User.has_perm \"django.contrib.auth.models.User.has_perm\") method, permission names take the form `\"<app label>.<permission codename>\"` (i.e. `polls.add_choice` for a permission on a model in the `polls` application).\n\nThe decorator may also take an iterable of permissions, in which case the user must have all of the permissions in order to access the view.\n\nNote that [`permission_required()`](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.permission_required \"django.contrib.auth.decorators.permission_required\") also takes an optional `login_url` parameter:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth.decorators import permission\\_required\n\n@permission\\_required(\"polls.add\\_choice\", login\\_url\\=\"/loginpage/\")\ndef my\\_view(request): ...\n\nAs in the [`login_required()`](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required \"django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required\") decorator, `login_url` defaults to [`settings.LOGIN_URL`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-LOGIN_URL).\n\nIf the `raise_exception` parameter is given, the decorator will raise [`PermissionDenied`](../../../ref/exceptions/#django.core.exceptions.PermissionDenied \"django.core.exceptions.PermissionDenied\"), prompting [the 403 (HTTP Forbidden) view](../../../ref/views/#http-forbidden-view) instead of redirecting to the login page.\n\nIf you want to use `raise_exception` but also give your users a chance to login first, you can add the [`login_required()`](#django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required \"django.contrib.auth.decorators.login_required\") decorator:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth.decorators import login\\_required, permission\\_required\n\n@login\\_required\n@permission\\_required(\"polls.add\\_choice\", raise\\_exception\\=True)\ndef my\\_view(request): ...\n\nThis also avoids a redirect loop when [`LoginView`](#django.contrib.auth.views.LoginView \"django.contrib.auth.views.LoginView\")’s `redirect_authenticated_user=True` and the logged-in user doesn’t have all of the required permissions.\n\nChanged in Django 5.1:\n\nSupport for wrapping asynchronous view functions was added.\n\n#### The `PermissionRequiredMixin` mixin[¶](#the-permissionrequiredmixin-mixin \"Link to this heading\")\n\nTo apply permission checks to [class-based views](../../../ref/class-based-views/), you can use the `PermissionRequiredMixin`:\n\n*class* PermissionRequiredMixin[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/mixins.py#L76)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.PermissionRequiredMixin \"Link to this definition\")\n\nThis mixin, just like the `permission_required` decorator, checks whether the user accessing a view has all given permissions. You should specify the permission (or an iterable of permissions) using the `permission_required` parameter:\n\nfrom django.contrib.auth.mixins import PermissionRequiredMixin\n\nclass MyView(PermissionRequiredMixin, View):\n    permission\\_required \\= \"polls.add\\_choice\"\n    \\# Or multiple of permissions:\n    permission\\_required \\= \\[\"polls.view\\_choice\", \"polls.change\\_choice\"\\]\n\nYou can set any of the parameters of [`AccessMixin`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin\") to customize the handling of unauthorized users.\n\nYou may also override these methods:\n\nget\\_permission\\_required()[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/mixins.py#L81)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.PermissionRequiredMixin.get_permission_required \"Link to this definition\")\n\nReturns an iterable of permission names used by the mixin. Defaults to the `permission_required` attribute, converted to a tuple if necessary.\n\nhas\\_permission()[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/mixins.py#L99)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.PermissionRequiredMixin.has_permission \"Link to this definition\")\n\nReturns a boolean denoting whether the current user has permission to execute the decorated view. By default, this returns the result of calling [`has_perms()`](../../../ref/contrib/auth/#django.contrib.auth.models.User.has_perms \"django.contrib.auth.models.User.has_perms\") with the list of permissions returned by [`get_permission_required()`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.PermissionRequiredMixin.get_permission_required \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.PermissionRequiredMixin.get_permission_required\").\n\n### Redirecting unauthorized requests in class-based views[¶](#redirecting-unauthorized-requests-in-class-based-views \"Link to this heading\")\n\nTo ease the handling of access restrictions in [class-based views](../../../ref/class-based-views/), the `AccessMixin` can be used to configure the behavior of a view when access is denied. Authenticated users are denied access with an HTTP 403 Forbidden response. Anonymous users are redirected to the login page or shown an HTTP 403 Forbidden response, depending on the [`raise_exception`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.raise_exception \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.raise_exception\") attribute.\n\n*class* AccessMixin[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/mixins.py#L10)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin \"Link to this definition\")\n\nlogin\\_url[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.login_url \"Link to this definition\")\n\nDefault return value for [`get_login_url()`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.get_login_url \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.get_login_url\"). Defaults to `None` in which case [`get_login_url()`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.get_login_url \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.get_login_url\") falls back to [`settings.LOGIN_URL`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-LOGIN_URL).\n\npermission\\_denied\\_message[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.permission_denied_message \"Link to this definition\")\n\nDefault return value for [`get_permission_denied_message()`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.get_permission_denied_message \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.get_permission_denied_message\"). Defaults to an empty string.\n\nredirect\\_field\\_name[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.redirect_field_name \"Link to this definition\")\n\nDefault return value for [`get_redirect_field_name()`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.get_redirect_field_name \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.get_redirect_field_name\"). Defaults to `\"next\"`.\n\nraise\\_exception[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.raise_exception \"Link to this definition\")\n\nIf this attribute is set to `True`, a [`PermissionDenied`](../../../ref/exceptions/#django.core.exceptions.PermissionDenied \"django.core.exceptions.PermissionDenied\") exception is raised when the conditions are not met. When `False` (the default), anonymous users are redirected to the login page.\n\nget\\_login\\_url()[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/mixins.py#L21)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.get_login_url \"Link to this definition\")\n\nReturns the URL that users who don’t pass the test will be redirected to. Returns [`login_url`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.login_url \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.login_url\") if set, or [`settings.LOGIN_URL`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-LOGIN_URL) otherwise.\n\nget\\_permission\\_denied\\_message()[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/mixins.py#L34)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.get_permission_denied_message \"Link to this definition\")\n\nWhen [`raise_exception`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.raise_exception \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.raise_exception\") is `True`, this method can be used to control the error message passed to the error handler for display to the user. Returns the [`permission_denied_message`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.permission_denied_message \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.permission_denied_message\") attribute by default.\n\nget\\_redirect\\_field\\_name()[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/mixins.py#L40)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.get_redirect_field_name \"Link to this definition\")\n\nReturns the name of the query parameter that will contain the URL the user should be redirected to after a successful login. If you set this to `None`, a query parameter won’t be added. Returns the [`redirect_field_name`](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.redirect_field_name \"django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.redirect_field_name\") attribute by default.\n\nhandle\\_no\\_permission()[\\[source\\]](https://github.com/django/django/blob/stable/5.2.x/django/contrib/auth/mixins.py#L46)[¶](#django.contrib.auth.mixins.AccessMixin.handle_no_permission \"Link to this definition\")\n\nDepending on the value of `raise_exception`, the method either raises a [`PermissionDenied`](../../../ref/exceptions/#django.core.exceptions.PermissionDenied \"django.core.exceptions.PermissionDenied\") exception or redirects the user to the `login_url`, optionally including the `redirect_field_name` if it is set.\n\n#### Session invalidation on password change[¶](#session-invalidation-on-password-change \"Link to this heading\")\n\nIf your [`AUTH_USER_MODEL`](../../../ref/settings/#std-setting-AUTH_USER_MODEL) inherits from [`AbstractBaseUser`](../customizing/#django.contrib.auth.models.AbstractBaseUser \"django.contrib.auth.models.AbstractBaseUser\") or implements its own [`get_session_auth_hash()`](../customizing/#django.contrib.auth.models.AbstractBaseUser.get_session_auth_hash \"django.contrib.auth.models.AbstractBaseUser.get_session_auth_hash\") method, authenticated sessions will include the hash returned by this function. In the [`AbstractBaseUser`](../customizing/#django.contrib.auth.models.AbstractBaseUser \"django.contrib.auth.models.AbstractBaseUser\") case, this is an HMAC of the password field. Django verifies that the hash in the session for each request matches the one that’s computed during the request.
